L22: 
L23: Templates are a special kind of cite6†alternate file. The template content and host specific data are combined as input to a template processor which produces a new file as its output.
L24: 
L25: This can be very useful if you need to vary a small part of a file, but it doesn’t support any kind of include directive.
L26: ## Template suffixes
L27: 
L28: To create a template, append an alternate suffix to the file name. The suffix has the format:
L29: 
L30:     `##template.<template processor>
L31:     `
L32: 
L33: _{^{ “template” can also be shortened to “t”. }}
L34: 
L35: The supported template processors are:
L36: Processor  | Suffixes  | Dependencies
L37: --- | --- | ---
L38: default  | `##template`, `##template.default`  | `awk` must be installed. (This should be installed on all *nix systems)
L39: esh  | `##template.esh`  | `esh` must be installed.
L40: j2cli  | `##template.j2`, `##template.j2cli`  | `j2cli` must be installed.
L41: envtpl  | `##template.j2`, `##template.envtpl`  | `envtpl` must be installed.
L42: 
L43: The processor can be omitted for “default”. Also, `j2` will be processed by either j2cli or envtpl, whichever is found.
L44: ## Exposed data
L45: 
L46: When template processors run, they will be provided the following set of data.
L47: Default (built-in)  | Jinja or ESH  | Description  | Source
L48: --- | --- | --- | ---
L49: `yadm.arch`  | `YADM_ARCH`  | Architecture  | `uname -m`
L50: `yadm.class`  | `YADM_CLASS`  | Last defined class  | `yadm config local.class`
L51: `yadm.classes`  | `YADM_CLASSES`  | All classes  | `yadm config --get-all local.class`
L52: `yadm.distro`  | `YADM_DISTRO`  | Distribution  | `lsb_release -si`
L53: or `/etc/os-release`
L54: `yadm.distro_family`  | `YADM_DISTRO_FAMILY`  | Distribution family  | `ID_LIKE` from`/etc/os-release`
L55: `yadm.filename`  |    | Current filename  | (fully qualified path) ^{*}
L56: `yadm.hostname`  | `YADM_HOSTNAME`  | Hostname  | `uname -n` (without domain)
L57: `yadm.os`  | `YADM_OS`  | Operating system  | `uname -s` ^{*}
L58: `yadm.source`  | `YADM_SOURCE`  | Template filename  | (fully qualified path)
L59: `yadm.user`  | `YADM_USER`  | Current user  | `id -u -n`
L60: `env.VAR`  |    | Env variables  | Any VAR in the environment while yadm templates are processed
L61: _{^{* Current filename differ from template filename in included files.
L62: * The OS for “Windows Subsystem for Linux” is reported as “WSL”, even though uname identifies as “Linux”.
L63: * If `lsb_release` is not available, “distro” will be the ID specified in `/etc/os-release`. }}
L64: ## Supported template processors
L65: default
L66:     This built-in processor requires no additional software (assuming your distro contains `awk`). This processor has a syntax similar to the Jinja processors below, however it only supports a small set of directives. Those directives are detailed in the section below.
L67: esh
L68:     cite15†esh†github.com is a template processor written in POSIX compliant shell. It allows executing shell commands within templates. This can be used to reference your own configurations within templates.
L69: j2cli
L70:     cite16†j2cli†github.com (or `j2`) is a Python-based Jinja2 template processor. This fully supports all directives of the cite17†Jinja2 library†jinja.palletsprojects.com . When your template is processed, the YADM_* values are provided to j2cli as environment variables.
L71: envtpl
L72:     cite18†envtpl†github.com is another Python-based Jinja2 template processor. Online comments suggest this software might not be maintained anymore.
L73: ## Built-in directives
L74: 
L75: yadm’s “default” (built-in) template processor supports the following directives.
L76: 
L77: variables
L78:     Variables should be surrounded by `{{ }}`. It is fine for there to be whitespace between the variable name and the double braces. The `{{` and `}}` must be on the same line. For example:
L79: 
L80:     `# WARNING: Do not edit this file.
L81:     # It was generated by processing {{ yadm.source }}
L82:     `
L83: if-else-endif
L84:     Entire blocks of content can be included or excluded based on the value of a variable. Both equality (`==`) and inequality (`!=`) can be tested. These blocks must start with `{% if yadm.variable == "value" %}` and end with `{% endif %}`. An alternative block can also be specified using the directive `{% else %}`. These directives must appear on lines by themselves. They may not appear on the same line.
L85: The “if” directive only supports testing a single variable, and there is no “elif” directive as there is in Jinja. Comparisons are done case-insensitive.
L86: If multiple classes are defined, `yadm.class=="someclass"` will be true if any of the defined classes are “someclass”.
L87: Here is an example.
L88: 
L89:     `{% if yadm.os == "Darwin" %}
L90:     This block is included for MacOS
L91:     {% else %}
L92:     This block is included for any other OS
L93:     {% endif %}
L94:     `
L95: include
L96:     Content can be included from external files using the `{% include "filename" %}` syntax. The filename may include variables and should be either a path relative to the current template or an absolute path. The included file may itself also use variables, if-else-endif and include directives. An example:
L97: 
L98:     `{% include "extra/config.{{ yadm.os }}" %}
L99:     `

L22: 
L23: Often there is more to set up once your dotfiles repository has been cloned. For example, if your repository has submodules, you may wish to initialize them. On MacOS, you may wish to install Homebrew and process a `.Brewfile`. These types of additional steps are generally referred to as “bootstrapping”.
L24: 
L25: Though everyone may have a different set of bootstrap operations they need to perform, yadm has a standard command for executing them.
L26: 
L27:     `yadm bootstrap
L28:     `
L29: This command will execute the program named `$HOME/.config/yadm/bootstrap`. You must provide this program yourself, and it must be made executable. But those are the only constraints.
L30: 
L31: After yadm successfully clones a repository, if there is a bootstrap program available, it will offer to run it for you.
L32: 
L33:     `Found .config/yadm/bootstrap
L34:     It appears that a bootstrap program exists.
L35:     Would you like to execute it now? (y/n)
L36:     `
L37: You can prevent this prompting by using the `--bootstrap` or `--no-bootstrap` options when cloning.
L38: 
L39: It is best to make the logic of your bootstrap idempotent—allowing it to be re-run in the future when you merge changes made on other hosts.
L40: ## Examples
L41: 
L42: Curious about the possibilities? See some examples below. These are all written in Bash, but you can use any executable file as a bootstrap.
L43: ### Initialize submodules
L44: 
L45: If you’ve added repositories as submodules for the yadm repository, you can initialize them after a successful clone.
L46: 
L47:     `#!/bin/sh
L48: 
L49:     # Because Git submodule commands cannot operate without a work tree, they must
L50:     # be run from within $HOME (assuming this is the root of your dotfiles)
L51:     cd "$HOME"
L52: 
L53:     echo "Init submodules"
L54:     yadm submodule update --recursive --init
L55:     `
L56: ### Install cite15†Homebrew†brew.sh and a bundle of recipes
L57: 
L58:     `#!/bin/sh
L59: 
L60:     system_type=$(uname -s)
L61: 
L62:     if [ "$system_type" = "Darwin" ]; then
L63: 
L64:       # install homebrew if it's missing
L65:       if ! command -v brew >/dev/null 2>&1; then
L66:         echo "Installing homebrew"
L67:         /bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"
L68:       fi
L69: 
L70:       if [ -f "$HOME/.Brewfile" ]; then
L71:         echo "Updating homebrew bundle"
L72:         brew bundle --global
L73:       fi
L74: 
L75:     fi
L76:     `
L77: ### Configure cite16†iTerm2†www.iterm2.com to use your configuration
L78: 
L79:     `#!/bin/sh
L80: 
L81:     system_type=$(uname -s)
L82: 
L83:     if [ "$system_type" = "Darwin" ]; then
L84: 
L85:       # possibly add something here to ensure iTerm2 is installed using Homebrew
L86:       # cask like in the previous example
L87: 
L88:       if [ -d "$HOME/.iterm2" ]; then
L89:         echo "Setting iTerm preference folder"
L90:         defaults write com.googlecode.iterm2 PrefsCustomFolder "$HOME/.iterm2"
L91:       fi
L92: 
L93:     fi
L94:     `
L95: ### Compile a custom terminfo file
L96: 
L97:     `#!/bin/sh
L98: 
L99:     if [ -f "$HOME/.terminfo/custom.terminfo" ]; then
L100:       echo "Updating terminfo"
L101:       tic "$HOME/.terminfo/custom.terminfo"
L102:     fi
L103:     `
L104: ### Update the yadm repo origin URL
L105: 
L106: You might initially clone your repo using `https`, but ssh configurations may be available after cloning. If so, you could update the yadm repo origin to use `ssh` instead.
L107: 
L108:     `#!/bin/sh
L109: 
L110:     echo "Updating the yadm repo origin URL"
L111:     yadm remote set-url origin "git@github.com:MyUser/dotfiles.git"
L112:     `
L113: ### Install cite17†vim†www.vim.org plugins managed with cite18†vim-plug†github.com L114: vim-plug can be used in your `.vimrc` to enable plugins. The example here will automatically download vim-plug and run the `:PlugInstall` command if vim-plug is missing when vim starts.
L115: 
L116:     `" download vim-plug if missing
L117:     if empty(glob("~/.vim/autoload/plug.vim"))
L118:       silent! execute '!curl --create-dirs -fsSLo ~/.vim/autoload/plug.vim https://raw.github.com/junegunn/vim-plug/master/plug.vim'
L119:       autocmd VimEnter * silent! PlugInstall
L120:     endif
L121: 
L122:     " declare plugins
L123:     silent! if plug#begin()
L124: 
L125:       Plug 'airblade/vim-gitgutter'
L126:       Plug 'c9s/perlomni.vim', { 'for': 'perl' }
L127:       Plug 'ctrlpvim/ctrlp.vim'
L128:       Plug 'vim-syntastic/syntastic'
L129:       Plug 'yggdroot/indentLine'
L130: 
L131:       " ignore these on older versions of vim
L132:       if v:version >= 703
L133:         Plug 'gorodinskiy/vim-coloresque'
L134:         Plug 'jamessan/vim-gnupg'
L135:       endif
L136:       if v:version >= 704
L137:         Plug 'vim-pandoc/vim-pandoc-syntax'
L138:       endif
L139: 
L140:       call plug#end()
L141:     endif
L142:     `
L143: You can enhance this scheme by having your bootstrap program initialize vim-plug when you clone, instead of when you first run vim. This example will install any new plugins, and also remove any plugins now deleted from your `.vimrc`.
L144: 
L145:     `#!/bin/sh
L146: 
L147:     if command -v vim >/dev/null 2>&1; then
L148:       echo "Bootstraping Vim"
L149:       vim '+PlugUpdate' '+PlugClean!' '+PlugUpdate' '+qall'
L150:     fi
L151:     `
L152: ### Bootstrap directory
L153: 
L154: By installing this cite19†contributed bootstrap†raw.githubusercontent.com script as the bootstrap program, it is possible to split the bootstrap process into separate scripts. Each script is placed in `$HOME/.config/yadm/bootstrap.d` and it is possible to use the cite6†alternate files system to control which systems that a specific bootstrap step is executed on.
L155: 
L156: * * *
L157: 
L158: If you have suggestions for useful bootstrapping logic, let me know…

Most tools converge on four patterns. Also, chezmoi does support this today through `modify_` scripts—its documentation specifically calls out managing part of a file.

| Approach | Used by | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| Whole-file templates | yadm, Home Manager, chezmoi | Generate and replace the complete file |
| Transform current contents | chezmoi `modify_` | Read current file on stdin, emit the desired complete file |
| Narrow text operations | Ansible | Ensure a line or marker-delimited block exists |
| Idempotent scripts/native commands | yadm, Dotbot, Home Manager | Run `sed`, `kwriteconfig6`, `defaults`, etc. |

Chezmoi

Chezmoi’s `modify_` scripts receive the current target contents on stdin and produce the updated contents on stdout. They can be ordinary scripts or templates with access to `.chezmoi.stdin`. It even documents structured updates for JSON, TOML, and YAML; for mixed-state INI files, it points to a third-party modify manager. [Chezmoi partial-file documentation](https://www.chezmoi.io/user-guide/manage-different-types-of-file/)

This is powerful enough for KDE, but has costs:

- The transform must be idempotent.
- A buggy transform can rewrite the whole file.
- Ownership and unapply behavior are unclear.
- Formatting, comments, and ordering may churn after parsing and serializing.

Ansible

Ansible provides the cleanest declarative vocabulary:

- [`lineinfile`](https://docs.ansible.com/projects/ansible/latest/collections/ansible/builtin/lineinfile_module.html) ensures or replaces a line and supports insertion positions.
- [`blockinfile`](https://docs.ansible.com/projects/ansible/latest/collections/ansible/builtin/blockinfile_module.html) owns marker-delimited blocks.
- [`ini_file`](https://docs.ansible.com/projects/ansible/latest/collections/community/general/ini_file_module.html) owns individual section/key/value settings.

Mise’s existing `line` and `block` edits are essentially the first two. Adding prepend positioning would bring `line` close to Ansible’s model.

yadm and Dotbot

Yadm templates still generate complete files. Anything more surgical goes into an idempotent bootstrap program. Yadm explicitly recommends making bootstrap scripts safe to rerun. [Yadm templates](https://yadm.io/docs/templates), [Yadm bootstrap](https://yadm.io/docs/bootstrap)

Dotbot similarly provides links plus arbitrary shell commands and plugins, while recommending idempotent setup. [Dotbot documentation](https://github.com/anishathalye/dotbot)

Home Manager

Home Manager normally owns generated files or exposes application-specific structured options. For anything outside its model, it provides ordered activation scripts that must be idempotent and support dry runs. [Home Manager activation options](https://nix-community.github.io/home-manager/options/home-manager/home.html)

My recommendation for mise:

- Add `prepend`/`append` positioning to the existing exact-line edit.
- Keep marker-delimited blocks.
- For KDE today, recommend a bootstrap hook invoking `kwriteconfig6`, which understands KConfig semantics.
- Consider a structured INI/KConfig edit only if there is significant demand.
- Avoid adding arbitrary “template the current file into a new file” transforms initially. Mise tasks/hooks already provide that escape hatch without making the declarative dotfiles model harder to reason about.

So templates remain appropriate for files mise owns completely. Partial management is better modeled as small declarative edits or application-native commands.

content.text:
PR opened: [#12941 — feat(bootstrap): allow prepending managed dotfile lines](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/12941). It’s ready for review; CI is running.

Suggested Discord response:

> mise already supports partial file edits using managed blocks and exact lines; templates are still for whole-file generation. I opened a PR adding prepend support for your `/etc/zshrc` case:
>
> ```toml
> [dotfiles]
> "/etc/zshrc/zdotdir" = {
>   line = 'ZDOTDIR=$HOME/.config/zsh/'
>   position = "prepend"
> }
> ```
>
> If that exact line already exists, mise leaves it alone. Otherwise it prepends it without changing the rest of the file.
>
